questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: The diagram shows a positive charge Q with dotted lines showing equipotential surfaces. [Diagram: +Q at the centre of three concentric dashed equipotential circles. P is on the outer circle at the right. Path X goes radially inward from P to the innermost circle. Path Y follows the outer circle a quarter turn to the top, then goes radially inward to the middle circle. Path Z follows the outer circle three-quarters of the way round to the left, then goes radially inward to the middle circle.] A small positive charge is moved from point P closer to the charge Q along three different paths X, Y and Z. The work done along each path is $W_X$, $W_Y$ and $W_Z$. Which relationship is correct? A $W_Z > W_Y > W_X$ B $W_X > W_Y = W_Z$ C $W_X = W_Y = W_Z$ D $W_Z = W_Y > W_X$

stemImage.alt: Question 19: The diagram shows a positive charge Q with dotted lines showing equipotential surfaces. A small positive charge is moved from point P closer to the charge Q alo

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires reading start and end equipotentials of each path and knowing work is path-independent.
questions.misconception: Thinking work done depends on the length of the path taken

explanation.body:
Movement along an equipotential surface involves zero work done, so only the radial parts of each path matter.

Paths Y and Z both end on the same (middle) equipotential, so $W_Y = W_Z$. Path X ends on the inner equipotential, closer to Q, so $W_X$ is larger.

perOption.A: Assumes longer paths need more work, but work depends only on the start and end potentials.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Path X ends at a higher potential than Y and Z, so more work is needed.
perOption.D: Inverts the comparison; X goes closer to Q, so it needs more work.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: The graph shows the variation of the electric potential $V$ with distance $x$ from a charged sphere. The radius of the sphere is $R$. [Graph: $V$ against $x$ starting at $x = R$, decreasing curve flattening out; point P on the curve at $x = D$ with potential $V_D$ marked by dashed lines.] What is the electric field strength at point P a distance $D$ from the centre? A $\frac{V_D}{D}$ B $-\frac{V_D}{D}$ C $\frac{dV}{dx}$ at P D $-\frac{dV}{dx}$ at P

stemImage.alt: Question 20: The graph shows the variation of the electric potential V with distance x from a charged sphere. The radius of the sphere is R. V P VD R D x What is the electri

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Recall that field strength is the negative potential gradient, read at a point on a graph.
questions.misconception: Using V/x instead of the gradient, or dropping the minus sign

explanation.body: Electric field strength at a point is equal to the negative potential gradient at that point: $E = -\dfrac{dV}{dx}$ at P.

perOption.A: $V/D$ is not the field; field depends on the gradient of $V$, not the ratio.
perOption.B: Still uses the ratio $V/D$ rather than the gradient.
perOption.C: Missing the negative sign; $V$ decreases with $x$, so $dV/dx$ is negative while $E$ points outward.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Four point charges of magnitude +2Q, +Q, –2Q, and –Q are fixed at the corners of a rigid square, resting on a frictionless surface.

A uniform electric field is applied in the direction from left to right in the plane of the surface.

In which situation will the square be in equilibrium?
questions.stemText: Four point charges of magnitude +2Q, +Q, –2Q, and –Q are fixed at the corners of a rigid square, resting on a frictionless surface. A uniform electric field is applied in the direction from left to right in the plane of the surface. In which situation will the square be in equilibrium? A –Q +2Q –2Q +Q B +2Q –2Q –Q +Q C –2Q +2Q +Q –Q D +Q +2Q –Q –2Q

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Must check both zero resultant force and zero resultant torque for four configurations.
questions.misconception: Thinking zero net force alone guarantees equilibrium

explanation.body: The field pushes positive charges to the right and negative charges to the left. In B, the forces on each horizontal pair are equal, opposite and collinear. The net force is zero and the clockwise and anticlockwise moments about the centre balance.

perOption.A: The net rightward force on the top row and net leftward force on the bottom row produce moments in the same sense.
perOption.B: Correct. The resultant force and resultant moment are both zero.
perOption.C: The top and bottom charges experience unequal leftward forces, so their opposing moments do not cancel.
perOption.D: The rightward top forces and leftward bottom forces turn the square in the same sense.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A small positively-charged particle P is balanced halfway between two horizontal plates when a potential difference V is applied between the plates.

When V is increased, P rises towards the upper plate.

When V is decreased, P falls towards the lower plate.

Which statement is correct?
questions.stemText: A small positively-charged particle P is balanced halfway between two horizontal plates when a potential difference V is applied between the plates. P V When V is increased, P rises towards the upper plate. When V is decreased, P falls towards the lower plate. Which statement is correct? A Decreasing V decreases both the electric and the gravitational potential energy of the particle. B Decreasing V increases the electric potential energy and decreases the gravitational potential energy of the particle. C Increasing V increases both the electric and the gravitational potential energy of the particle. D The change of electric potential energy of the particle must equal the change of gravitational potential energy of the particle.

options.label: A
options.text: Decreasing V decreases both the electric and the gravitational potential energy of the particle.

options.label: B
options.text: Decreasing V increases the electric potential energy and decreases the gravitational potential energy of the particle.

options.label: C
options.text: Increasing V increases both the electric and the gravitational potential energy of the particle.

options.label: D
options.text: The change of electric potential energy of the particle must equal the change of gravitational potential energy of the particle.

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires deducing the field direction from the balance, then tracking energy changes for a positive charge.
questions.misconception: Assuming electric and gravitational potential energy always change together or by equal amounts

explanation.body: The electric force must act upwards to balance the weight, so the upper plate is at lower potential. When $V$ is decreased, the particle falls towards the higher-potential lower plate. During that fall, the positive particle gains electric potential energy and loses gravitational potential energy.

perOption.A: During the fall, the positive particle moves towards higher electric potential.
perOption.B: Correct. During the fall, electric potential energy rises and gravitational potential energy falls.
perOption.C: During the rise, the positive particle moves towards lower electric potential.
perOption.D: After the voltage changes, the electric force and weight differ, so the energy changes need not have equal magnitudes.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Two point charges $+2q$ and $-q$ are situated along a line at a distance 0.90 m apart. A point P is at a distance 0.30 m from the charge $+2q$. [Diagram: $+2q$ on the left, P 0.30 m to its right, $-q$ a further 0.60 m to the right.] The magnitude of the electric field strength at P due to the $+2q$ charge alone is $24\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$. What is the magnitude of the resultant electric field strength at P due to both charges? A $18\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$ B $21\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$ C $27\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$ D $30\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$

stemImage.alt: Question 20: Two point charges +2q and −q are situated along a line at a distance 0.90 m apart. A point P is at a distance 0.30 m from the charge +2q. −q +2q P 0.30 m 0.60 m

appearances.originalFile: CJC PHY/H2/J2.H2.PRELIM.2026.Paper 1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires scaling E with Q/r² and combining field directions correctly.
questions.misconception: Subtracting the fields because the charges have opposite signs

explanation.body: The field from $+2q$ is $E_{2q}=2q/[4\pi\varepsilon_0(0.30)^2]=24\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$ to the right. The field from $-q$ is also to the right and has magnitude $q/[4\pi\varepsilon_0(0.60)^2]=E_{2q}/8=3\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$. Adding the two gives $27\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Subtracts the fields and treats the charge magnitudes as equal.
perOption.B: Subtracts the field of the negative charge even though both fields point right.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Treats the charges as equal in magnitude, doubling the negative charge's contribution.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A proton, initially travelling horizontally at $2.52\times10^6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, enters a uniform electric field at right angles to the field. The field is produced by a p.d. of 5.00 kV between two parallel plates 15.0 cm long and 10.0 cm apart. [Diagram: upper plate at 5.00 kV, lower plate at 0 V; proton enters horizontally midway between the plates.] What is the change in height of the proton as it leaves the plates and the direction in which it is deflected? A $8.5\times10^{-3}$ m, downwards B $8.5\times10^{-3}$ m, upwards C $15.6\times10^{-3}$ m, downwards D $15.6\times10^{-3}$ m, upwards

stemImage.alt: Question 23:  6 2.52 10 m s−1, enters a uniform electric field at A proton, initially travelling horizontally at right angles to the field. The electric field is generated

appearances.originalFile: DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Chained calculation: field, acceleration, time in plates, then deflection, plus direction reasoning.
questions.misconception: Using the plate separation as the distance travelled or reversing the force direction for a positive charge

explanation.body: The field points downwards from the $5.00\ \mathrm{kV}$ plate to the $0\ \mathrm V$ plate, so the positive proton experiences a downward force. Its magnitude is $F=qE=(1.60\times10^{-19})(5000/0.100)=8.00\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm N$. This gives $a=F/m=4.790\times10^{12}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, and the transit time is $t=L/v_x=0.150/(2.52\times10^6)=5.952\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm s$. Thus $y=\tfrac12at^2=8.49\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm m$, or $8.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm m$ downwards.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Reverses the direction of the force on the positive proton.
perOption.C: Overestimates the displacement from the downward acceleration and horizontal transit time.
perOption.D: Overestimates the displacement and reverses the force direction.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: Two point charges each of charge Q at a separation of r repel each other with a force F. Each charge is increased by adding 3Q and the separation is increased to 2r. What is the force between the charges?
questions.stemText: Two point charges each of charge Q at a separation of r repel each other with a force F. Each charge is increased by adding 3Q and the separation is increased to 2r. What is the force between the charges? A F B 9 F 4 C 4F D 8F

appearances.originalFile: DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Coulomb's law ratio with a small trap in reading 'adding 3Q'.
questions.misconception: Reading 'adding 3Q' as making the charge 3Q, or forgetting to square the distance

explanation.body: The original force is $F=kQ^2/r^2$. Each charge becomes $Q+3Q=4Q$ and the separation becomes $2r$, so $F_{\mathrm{new}}=k(4Q)(4Q)/(2r)^2=4kQ^2/r^2$. Hence $F_{\mathrm{new}}/F=4$.

perOption.A: Applies the charge increase to only one charge, making it cancel the factor of four from the distance.
perOption.B: Treats each new charge as $3Q$ instead of $4Q$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses an inverse-distance law instead of the inverse-square law.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A fixed charge is isolated in space. The electric potential at X, a distance of $1.2 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m}$ from the fixed charge, is $-1.2 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}$ as shown. [Diagram: point charge and point X separated by $1.2 \times 10^{-5}$ m] An α-particle passes through this point at one instant. What is the magnitude of the electric potential at the midpoint between the α-particle and the fixed charge at this instant? A $1.2 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}$ B $2.4 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}$ C $4.8 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}$ D $7.2 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}$

stemImage.alt: Question 19: − 5  1.2 10 m A fixed charge is isolated in space. The electric potential at X, a distance of − − 4 1 −  from the fixed charge, is as shown. 1.2 10 J C charge

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Must deduce the fixed charge is $-e$, then superpose potentials of opposite sign.
questions.misconception: Ignoring the alpha particle's own potential or adding magnitudes regardless of sign

explanation.body: The fixed charge’s potential doubles in magnitude at half the distance, giving $-2.4\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}$ at the midpoint. The given potential and distance imply a fixed charge of about $-e$, so the alpha particle’s charge of $+2e$ contributes $+4.8\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}$ there. Adding the signed potentials gives $+2.4\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses the magnitude of the fixed charge’s potential at X without calculating the net midpoint potential.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Includes only the alpha particle’s contribution.
perOption.D: Adds the magnitudes of the two contributions despite their opposite signs.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A capacitor is charged to a voltage V and then discharged through a small d.c. motor. As the capacitor discharges, the motor raises a mass through a height h. The experiment is repeated for several values of V.

A constant fraction of the capacitor energy is converted to gain of gravitational potential energy.

Which graph is expected to give a straight line?
questions.stemText: A capacitor is charged to a voltage V and then discharged through a small d.c. motor. As the capacitor discharges, the motor raises a mass through a height h. The experiment is repeated for several values of V. A constant fraction of the capacitor energy is converted to gain of gravitational potential energy. Which graph is expected to give a straight line? A h against V 2 B h against V C h against V D 1 h against V

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs only $E = \tfrac12 CV^2$ and $mgh$ proportional to it.
questions.misconception: Assuming energy stored is proportional to V rather than V²

explanation.body: The capacitor stores $\tfrac12 CV^2$. If a constant fraction $k$ becomes gravitational potential energy, then $mgh=k(\tfrac12 CV^2)$ and $h=\frac{kC}{2mg}V^2$. Thus a graph of $h$ against $V^2$ is a straight line.

perOption.A: Correct. The height is proportional to the squared voltage.
perOption.B: This treats $h$ as linear in $V$, though it is quadratic.
perOption.C: If the horizontal variable is $\sqrt V$, the height varies as its fourth power.
perOption.D: If the horizontal variable is $1/\sqrt V$, the height varies as its inverse fourth power.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Point charges, each of magnitude q, are arranged at the corners of a square.

For which arrangement will the magnitude of the resultant electric field strength at the centre of the square be the largest?
questions.stemText: Point charges, each of magnitude q, are arranged at the corners of a square. For which arrangement will the magnitude of the resultant electric field strength at the centre of the square be the largest? A  B  C  D

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires vector addition of four fields with careful attention to direction for each charge sign.
questions.misconception: Adding field magnitudes without direction, or thinking all like charges give the largest field

explanation.body: Each corner contributes the same field magnitude at the centre. The vectors cancel completely in A and B, while D leaves two aligned contributions. In C the vertical components cancel and all four horizontal components add, giving $4\cos45^\circ=2\sqrt2$ times the field from one corner, the largest resultant.

perOption.A: The fields from diagonally opposite charges cancel in pairs.
perOption.B: The equal-sign charges on each diagonal produce opposing fields that cancel.
perOption.C: Correct. All four horizontal components reinforce each other.
perOption.D: One diagonal pair cancels, leaving only two aligned fields.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: An electron is projected horizontally with a speed of $3.1\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. It passes in between the two charged horizontal plates. The uniform electric field between the plates is $20000\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$. As the electron pass through the plates, it is deflected. The time taken for the electron to travel the length of the plate is $4.0\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{s}$. [Diagram: two horizontal plates, upper at low potential, lower at high potential; electron enters horizontally from the left midway between them] What is the vertical distance travelled by the electron after it has travelled the length of the plate? A $1.76\times10^{-17}$ m B $7.85\times10^{-17}$ m C 0.0281 m D 0.152 m

stemImage.alt: Question 24: An electron is projected horizontally with a speed of 3.1  107 m s−1. It passes in between the two charged horizontal plates. The uniform electric field betwee

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires finding acceleration from $eE/m$ then applying uniform-acceleration kinematics.
questions.misconception: Using force instead of acceleration in the kinematics equation

explanation.body: The electric force gives a vertical acceleration of $a=F_E/m=|q|E/m=(1.6\times10^{-19})(20000)/(9.11\times10^{-31})=3.51\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. The initial vertical velocity is zero, so $s=ut+\frac12 at^2=\frac12(3.51\times10^{15})(4.0\times10^{-9})^2=0.0281\ \mathrm m$.

perOption.A: The vertical displacement must be calculated using the electron’s acceleration $|q|E/m$ and the squared transit time.
perOption.B: The field acting for $4.0\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm s$ produces a much larger displacement when the electron’s mass is included in the acceleration.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Adds the horizontal travel $vt$ to the vertical displacement.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: PQR is an equilateral triangle of sides $20\ \mathrm{cm}$. A $-30\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ charge and another $-30\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ charge are placed at points P and Q respectively. [Diagram: equilateral triangle PQR, side $20\ \mathrm{cm}$, $-30\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ at P and Q, R at the top vertex] What is the work done to move an electron to point R from infinity? A $-4.3\times10^{13}\ \mathrm{J}$ B $-2.7\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{J}$ C $2.7\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{J}$ D $4.3\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{J}$

stemImage.alt: Question 19: PQR is an equilateral triangle of sides 20 cm. A –30 C charge and another –30 C charge are placed at points P and Q respectively. R 20 cm 20 cm –30 C –30 C 20

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Summing scalar potentials and multiplying by a negative charge with care over signs.
questions.misconception: Sign error from forgetting the electron's negative charge

explanation.body: The two charges each contribute $kq/r$ to the potential at R, so $V_R=2k(-30\times10^{-6})/0.20\approx-2.7\times10^6\ \mathrm{V}$. The work required from infinity is $\Delta U=(-e)V_R\approx4.3\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{J}$, where $e$ is the magnitude of the electron charge.

perOption.A: Has the wrong sign and power of ten for the work required to bring in the electron.
perOption.B: Uses the negative electric potential directly as the work.
perOption.C: Uses the magnitude of the electric potential as work without multiplying by the electron charge magnitude.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: W, X, Y and Z are four points on a square as shown. [Diagram: square with W top-left, X top-right, Y bottom-right, Z bottom-left] Two point charges each of charge $+Q$ are at W and X. Which of the following statements is true when the point charge at X is moved to Y while the charge at W remains fixed? A The electric potential at Z will decrease. B The electric potential energy of the system will increase. C The repulsive force between the two charges will increase. D The magnitude of the electric field strength at Z will increase.

stemImage.alt: Question 20: 4.3 × 10–13 J A B C D W, X, Y and Z are four points on a square as shown. X W A Z Y Two point charges each of charge +Q are at W and X. Which of the following s

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Option D needs a vector sum of fields at Z before and after; the difference is small.
questions.misconception: Assuming field strength at Z must decrease because one charge moves

explanation.body: For square side $r$, the fields at Z from W and X initially have magnitudes $kQ/r^2$ and $kQ/(2r^2)$, with $45^\circ$ between them. The cosine rule gives an initial resultant of about $1.399kQ/r^2$. At Y, the moved charge produces a field at Z of magnitude $kQ/r^2$ perpendicular to W’s field, so the resultant rises to about $1.414kQ/r^2$.

perOption.A: The moved charge is closer to Z, so the potential there increases.
perOption.B: The charges are farther apart, so their potential energy decreases.
perOption.C: The charges are farther apart, so their repulsive force decreases.
perOption.D: Correct. The resultant field at Z increases.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A capacitor is charged by a constant current of 2.5 µA for 200 s. As a result, the potential difference across the capacitor increases by 5.0 V.

What is the capacitance of the capacitor?
questions.stemText: A capacitor is charged by a constant current of 2.5 µA for 200 s. As a result, the potential difference across the capacitor increases by 5.0 V. What is the capacitance of the capacitor? A 40 µF B 100 µF C 40 mF D 100 mF

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: One substitution of Q = It into C = Q/V with prefix handling.
questions.misconception: Prefix or power-of-ten slip with micro/milli

explanation.body: The charge added is $Q=It=(2.5\times10^{-6})(200)=5.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{C}$. Dividing by the voltage increase gives $C=Q/\Delta V=(5.0\times10^{-4})/5.0=100\ \mathrm{\mu F}$.

perOption.A: Gives too little capacitance to store the calculated charge at the stated voltage increase.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses millifarads and also gives the wrong numerical value in microfarads.
perOption.D: Uses millifarads for a value calculated in microfarads.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A point X is surrounded symmetrically by six positive charges $+Q$ and two negative charges $-Q$ at distance $r$ as shown. [Diagram: eight point charges equally spaced on a circle of radius $r$ centred on X; six are $+Q$ and two (at left-upper and right-lower positions) are $-Q$.] How much work is done by the electric field to bring a point charge of $+2Q$ from infinity to position X? A $-\frac{Q^2}{\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$ B $-\frac{2Q^2}{\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$ C $\frac{2Q^2}{\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$ D $-\frac{4Q^2}{\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$

stemImage.alt: Question 19: A point X is surrounded symmetrically by six positive charges +Q and two negative charges −Q at distance r as shown. +Q +Q − Q +Q r X +Q − Q +Q +Q How much work

appearances.originalFile: NYJC/H2/2026 NYJC H2 Phy 9478 P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs scalar superposition of potentials and the sign convention for work done by the field.
questions.misconception: Confusing work done by the field with work done by an external agent

explanation.body: Electric potential is a scalar, so at X it is $V=6\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}+2\frac{-Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}=\frac{Q}{\pi\varepsilon_0r}$. The external work to bring in $+2Q$ equals the increase in potential energy, $(2Q)V=\frac{2Q^2}{\pi\varepsilon_0r}$. The field does the negative of this work, $-\frac{2Q^2}{\pi\varepsilon_0r}$.

perOption.A: Uses $+Q$ for the incoming charge instead of $+2Q$.
perOption.B: Correct. The field does negative work as potential energy increases.
perOption.C: Gives the work done by the external force.
perOption.D: Treats the two negative charges as positive when summing the potentials.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: What is the electrostatic force between a thorium nucleus of charge $1.4\times10^{-17}$ C and an alpha particle when they are separated by a distance of 0.10 pm? A $4.0\times10^{-20}$ N B $4.0\times10^{-13}$ N C 4.0 N D 8.0 N

stemImage.alt: Question 20: What is the electrostatic force between a thorium nucleus of charge 1.4  10−17 C and an alpha particle when they are separated by a distance of 0.10 pm?

appearances.originalFile: NYJC/H2/2026 NYJC H2 Phy 9478 P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Single Coulomb's-law substitution, with care over the pico prefix and alpha charge.
questions.misconception: Using the electron charge for the alpha particle or mis-converting pm

explanation.body: The alpha particle has charge $+2e$ and the separation is $0.10\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}$. Coulomb’s law gives $F=\frac{(1.4\times10^{-17})(2\times1.6\times10^{-19})}{4\pi(8.85\times10^{-12})(0.10\times10^{-12})^2}=4.0\ \mathrm N$.

perOption.A: Uses the numerical distance in picometres without converting to metres.
perOption.B: Divides by the separation only once instead of squaring it.
perOption.C: Correct. The force is repulsive.
perOption.D: Uses $+4e$ for the alpha particle instead of $+2e$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The diagram shows the magnitude of the electric field strength at distances from an isolated point charge Q.

[Diagram: a square grid with point charge Q at a grid intersection. A point one square directly below Q is labelled 32.0 N C$^{-1}$. A point one square up and one square right of Q is labelled 16.0 N C$^{-1}$. Point R is one square up and two squares right of Q. Point S is three squares to the right of Q, on the same horizontal line.]

The electric field strength is given at points on grid lines at different distances from Q. The grid lines have equal separation.

What is the electric field strength at the two points marked R and S?

| | field strength at R / N C$^{-1}$ | field strength at S / N C$^{-1}$ |
|---|---|---|
| A | 4.0 | 3.6 |
| B | 6.4 | 1.8 |
| C | 6.4 | 3.6 |
| D | 8.0 | 4.0 |

stemImage.alt: Question 20: The diagram shows the magnitude of the electric field strength at distances from an isolated point charge Q. −1 16.0 N C R Q S −1 32.0 N C The electric field st

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must read the distances off a grid (including diagonals) and apply the inverse square law.

explanation.body:
Let $r$ be the side of one grid square. The 32.0 N C$^{-1}$ point is $r$ from Q:

$E = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2} = 32.0$

S is $3r$ from Q: $E_S = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 (3r)^2} = \tfrac{1}{9}(32.0) = 3.6\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$

Check: the 16.0 N C$^{-1}$ point is $\sqrt{2}r$ away, giving $\tfrac{1}{2}E = 16.0\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$.

R is $\sqrt{(2r)^2 + r^2} = \sqrt{5}r$ away: $E_R = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0(\sqrt{5}r)^2} = \tfrac{1}{5}E = 6.4\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$

perOption.A: Takes R as $\sqrt{8}r$ away (two squares across and two up), giving $\tfrac{1}{8} \times 32 = 4.0$ for R.
perOption.B: Gets R right, but gives half the correct value at S.
perOption.C: Correct. $E \propto 1/r^2$, with R at $\sqrt{5}r$ and S at $3r$.
perOption.D: Uses $E \propto 1/r$ or miscounts the distances, rather than $E \propto 1/r^2$ with the correct geometry.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An isolated hollow metal sphere with centre O and radius r carries a positive charge.

Which graph shows the variation with distance x from O of the electric potential V along OX?
questions.stemText: An isolated hollow metal sphere with centre O and radius r carries a positive charge. r O X positively charged hollow sphere Which graph shows the variation with distance x from O of the electric potential V along OX? A V 0 r x B V 0 r x C V 0 r x D V 0 r x

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: A standard result, though students often confuse zero field with zero potential.
questions.misconception: Zero electric field inside implies zero potential inside

explanation.body:
The sphere is a conductor, so its charge sits only on the outer surface and there is no charge inside. The electric field inside is therefore zero, and the potential inside is constant at $V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{Q}{r}$, the same as the potential at the surface.

Outside the sphere, the potential decreases inversely with the distance $x$ from the centre: $V \propto \dfrac{1}{x}$.

perOption.A: Takes the potential inside to be zero, confusing it with the electric field strength, which is zero inside.
perOption.B: Shows the potential rising from zero inside, but $E = 0$ inside means $V$ cannot change there.
perOption.C: Shows $V$ rising linearly inside, as if the field inside were non-zero.
perOption.D: Correct. $V$ is constant inside and equal to the surface value, then falls as $1/x$ outside.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Two fixed point charges +2Q and -Q are separated by a distance 2d.

A particle of mass m and charge +q approaches from a large distance with speed u. It subsequently passes through the midpoint M between the two fixed charges.

Assume that the fixed charges remain stationary, what is the speed of the particle as it passes through M?
questions.stemText: Two fixed point charges +2Q and -Q are separated by a distance 2d. A particle of mass m and charge +q approaches from a large distance with speed u. It subsequently passes through the midpoint M between the two fixed charges. Assume that the fixed charges remain stationary, what is the speed of the particle as it passes through M? A Qq − u 2 2  md 0 B Qq u − 2 2  md 0 C Qq − u 2 4  md 0 D Qq u − 2 4  md 0

appearances.originalFile: RVHS/RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Add the signed potential energies of both charge pairs and then conserve energy.
questions.misconception: Losing the sign or factor of two in the kinetic energy change

explanation.body: At M the particle has electric potential energy $U=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\frac{2Qq}{d}-\frac{Qq}{d}\right)=\frac{Qq}{4\pi\varepsilon_0d}$. By conservation of energy, the kinetic energy lost equals this gain, so $\tfrac12mu^2-\tfrac12mv^2=U$. Hence $v=\sqrt{u^2-\frac{Qq}{2\pi\varepsilon_0md}}$.

perOption.A: This reverses the order of subtraction under the square root.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: This reverses the subtraction and misses the factor of two when converting the energy gain into a change in squared speed.
perOption.D: This misses the factor of two when converting the energy gain into a change in squared speed.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A potential difference is applied between two metal plates that are not parallel.

Which diagram shows the electric field between the plates?
questions.stemText: A potential difference is applied between two metal plates that are not parallel. Which diagram shows the electric field between the plates? A  B  C  D

appearances.originalFile: RVHS/RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Check both the angle of the field lines at the plates and how their spacing changes.
questions.misconception: Drawing field lines that meet conductors obliquely

explanation.body: Each metal plate is an equipotential surface, so the electric field lines meet it at right angles. The plates are farther apart at the top, where the field is weaker and the lines are more widely spaced.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: The straight, evenly spaced lines meet the plates obliquely and imply a uniform field.
perOption.C: The even spacing misses the stronger field at the narrow end.
perOption.D: The spacing changes appropriately, but the straight lines meet the plates obliquely.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An oil drop of mass 2.6 × $10^{-15}$ kg and with a charge of – 4.8 × $10^{-19}$ C is in a vacuum between two horizontal plates. The plates have a separation of 2.0 cm and a potential difference between them of 1200 V, as shown.

Which statement describes the motion of the oil drop?
questions.stemText: An oil drop of mass 2.6 × 10–15 kg and with a charge of – 4.8 × 10–19 C is in a vacuum between two horizontal plates. The plates have a separation of 2.0 cm and a potential difference between them of 1200 V, as shown. Which statement describes the motion of the oil drop? A It is stationary. B It has a downward acceleration of 9.7 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$. C It has an upward acceleration of 1.3 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$. D It has an upward acceleration of 11 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$.

options.label: B
options.text: It has a downward acceleration of 9.7 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$.

options.label: C
options.text: It has an upward acceleration of 1.3 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$.

options.label: D
options.text: It has an upward acceleration of 11 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$.

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires finding the electric force and subtracting weight before calculating acceleration.
questions.misconception: Ignoring weight in the net force

explanation.body: The drop’s weight is $mg=(2.6\times10^{-15})(9.81)=2.55\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{N}$. The field has magnitude $E=V/d=1200/0.02=60\,000\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, giving the negative drop an upward electric force of $2.88\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{N}$. The net force is upward, so $a=(2.88-2.55)\times10^{-14}/(2.6\times10^{-15})\approx1.3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

perOption.A: Assumes the electric force and weight balance exactly.
perOption.B: Treats the drop as nearly in free fall even though the upward electric force exceeds its weight.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the electric force alone and neglects weight.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: An electron is released from rest in a uniform electric field. How will its electric potential energy and electric potential change?
questions.stemText: An electron is released from rest in a uniform electric field. How will its electric potential energy and electric potential change? A Potential energy increases, electric potential increases B Potential energy decreases, electric potential increases C Potential energy increases, electric potential decreases D Potential energy decreases, electric potential decreases

options.label: A
options.text: Potential energy increases, electric potential increases

options.label: B
options.text: Potential energy decreases, electric potential increases

options.label: C
options.text: Potential energy increases, electric potential decreases

options.label: D
options.text: Potential energy decreases, electric potential decreases

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires tracking the motion of a negative charge and the associated energy transfer.
questions.misconception: Assuming a negative charge moves toward lower potential

explanation.body: The electron is negatively charged, so the electric force acts opposite to the field and moves it towards higher electric potential. The field does positive work as the electron accelerates, increasing its kinetic energy. By energy conservation, its electric potential energy decreases.

perOption.A: Assumes increasing electric potential also increases the potential energy of a negative charge.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Treats the electron as moving along the field and gaining potential energy as it accelerates.
perOption.D: Assumes the electron follows the field towards lower potential, even though the force on it is opposite to the field.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A $20\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor is charged by a constant current of $10\ \mathrm{mA}$.

If the capacitor is initially uncharged, how long does it take for the potential difference across the capacitor to reach $300\ \mathrm{V}$?

A $6.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{s}$
B $0.60\ \mathrm{s}$
C $15\ \mathrm{s}$
D $1.5\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{s}$

stemImage.alt: Question 23: A 20 F capacitor is charged by a constant current of 10 mA. If the capacitor is initially uncharged, how long does it take for the potential difference across

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: It uses two short charge equations and a unit conversion.
questions.misconception: Confusing milliampere and ampere

explanation.body: At $300\ \mathrm{V}$, the stored charge is $Q=CV=(20\times10^{-6})(300)\ \mathrm{C}$. The current is constant, so $Q=It$ gives $t=(20\times10^{-6})(300)/(10\times10^{-3})=0.60\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Treats $10 mathrm{mA}$ as $10 mathrm{A}$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Does not use the charge required at $300 mathrm{V}$ divided by the given charging current.
perOption.D: Does not satisfy $It=CV$ for the specified voltage.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A positively charged oil droplet is held stationary in an electric field of strength E.

A different droplet of the same oil is held stationary in an electric field of different strength. The droplet has half the charge and twice the radius of the original droplet.

What is the electric field strength?
questions.stemText: A positively charged oil droplet is held stationary in an electric field of strength E. A different droplet of the same oil is held stationary in an electric field of different strength. The droplet has half the charge and twice the radius of the original droplet. What is the electric field strength? A 2E B 4E C 8E D 16E

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must scale the droplet’s volume and account for the reduced charge in the equilibrium equation.
questions.misconception: Droplet mass scales linearly with radius.

explanation.body: For the original stationary droplet, $qE=mg$. The oil density stays the same, so $m\propto r^3$ and doubling the radius gives $m_2=8m$. The second droplet has charge $q/2$, so $(q/2)E_2=8mg=8qE$. Cancelling $q$ gives $E_2=16E$.

perOption.A: Accounts for halving the charge but keeps the original weight.
perOption.B: Treats the mass as proportional to radius, giving only a factor of two in weight.
perOption.C: Accounts for the eightfold weight increase but keeps the original charge.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
In the diagrams, the thin lines show equipotential lines and the bold arrows show the electric field lines and their directions.

Which set of equipotential lines and field lines is correct?
questions.stemText: In the diagrams, the thin lines show equipotential lines and the bold arrows show the electric field lines and their directions. Which set of equipotential lines and field lines is correct? A 7 V 5 V 3 V B 7 V 5 V 3 V C 7 V 5 V 3 V D 7 V 5 V 3 V

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must check both the crossing angles and the direction of decreasing potential.
questions.misconception: Field lines can cross equipotentials obliquely.

explanation.body: Electric field lines are perpendicular to equipotentials at every crossing. They point from higher to lower potential, here from $7\ \mathrm{V}$ through $5\ \mathrm{V}$ to $3\ \mathrm{V}$. Only C satisfies both rules.

perOption.A: The arrows point towards lower potential but cross the outer equipotentials obliquely.
perOption.B: The arrows point towards higher potential and cross the outer equipotentials obliquely.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: The lines cross perpendicularly but the arrows point towards higher potential.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The electric potential and the electric field strength due to a point charge at distance $d$ from the charge is $V$ and $E$ respectively. What is the electric potential and the electric field strength at a distance $d/4$ from the point charge?
[Table columns are electric potential and electric field strength.]
A $4V$, $8E$
B $4V$, $16E$
C $8V$, $8E$
D $8V$, $16E$

stemImage.alt: Question 18: The electric potential and the electric field strength due to a point charge at distance d from the charge is V and E respectively. d from the point What is the

appearances.originalFile: TMJC/TMJC_2026_H2 Physics_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The student applies two familiar distance laws to the same change in separation.
questions.misconception: Confusing inverse-distance and inverse-square scaling

explanation.body: At distance $d$, $V=Q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0d)$ and $E=Q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0d^2)$. Replacing $d$ by $d/4$ gives $V_{\mathrm{new}}=Q/[4\pi\varepsilon_0(d/4)]=4V$. The field becomes $E_{\mathrm{new}}=Q/[4\pi\varepsilon_0(d/4)^2]=16E$.

perOption.A: Uses 8 as the field multiplier instead of squaring the distance factor of 4.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Overstates the potential multiplier and understates the inverse-square increase in field strength.
perOption.D: Applies a factor of 8 to the potential even though it scales inversely with distance.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Two point charges Q and R, are separated in a vacuum by a distance d as shown.

The variation with distance of x from charge Q of the net electric potential V between the two charges is shown below.

Which graph shows the variation with distance x of the net electric field strength E between the two charges?
questions.stemText: Two point charges Q and R, are separated in a vacuum by a distance d as shown. R Q d x The variation with distance of x from charge Q of the net electric potential V between the two charges is shown below. V / V V0 0 x Q R −V0 Which graph shows the variation with distance x of the net electric field strength E between the two charges? A E 0 Q R x B E 0 Q R x C E 0 Q R x D E 0 Q R x

appearances.originalFile: TMJC/TMJC_2026_H2 Physics_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The student must infer both the field direction and its changing strength from graph gradients.
questions.misconception: Equating zero potential with zero electric field

explanation.body: The electric field is the negative potential gradient, $E=-\mathrm dV/\mathrm dx$. The potential gradient is negative throughout, so the field is positive. Near the middle the slope has its smallest magnitude and remains nonzero, so the field has a positive minimum.

perOption.A: Confuses the zero of potential with a zero of its gradient.
perOption.B: Uses the wrong field sign and gives zero at a point where the slope remains nonzero.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the potential gradient itself, giving a negative field.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: The graph below shows how the electric field strength E varies with displacement x from a point A. What is the change in potential for an electron if it is moved from a point 3.0 m away from A
questions.stemText: The graph below shows how the electric field strength E varies with displacement x from a point A. What is the change in potential for an electron if it is moved from a point 3.0 m away from A to another point 5.0 m away from A? E / N C-1 E / N C-1 7.8 7.8 5.2 5.2 x / m x / m 0 3.0 5.0 3.0 5.0 A –13 V B –1.3 V C 1.3 V D 13 V

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Calculate the trapezium area and apply the negative sign in the potential gradient.
questions.misconception: Using the slope of the field graph or reversing the sign for an electron.

explanation.body: The field along the displacement is $E=-\mathrm{d}V/\mathrm{d}x$. Between $3.0$ and $5.0\ \mathrm{m}$, the area under the graph is $\tfrac12(7.8+5.2)(5.0-3.0)=13\ \mathrm{V}$. The field points in the direction of increasing $x$, so the potential decreases and $\Delta V=-13\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The potential change is the negative of the trapezium area.
perOption.B: Uses the slope of the field graph as the potential change.
perOption.C: Uses the magnitude of the slope instead of the negative area.
perOption.D: Uses the area with the wrong sign.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Two charges $+Q$ and $-2Q$ are placed at a distance $2d$ apart. Point X is at a distance $d$ away from the $-2Q$ charge as shown below.

[From left to right on one line: $+Q$, then $-2Q$ at distance $2d$, then X a further distance $d$ away.]

What is the electrical potential energy of a $+3Q$ charge placed at X?

A $\frac{5Q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0d}$
B $\frac{-5Q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0d}$
C $\frac{-Q^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0d^2}$
D $\frac{Q^2}{12\pi\varepsilon_0d^2}$

stemImage.alt: Question 19: Two charges + Q and –2Q are placed at a distance 2d apart. Point X is at a distance d away from the −2Q charge as shown below: 2d d +Q – 2Q X 11 What is the ele

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Add the signed potentials from two charges at different distances, then multiply by the test charge.
questions.misconception: Using the inverse-square field law for potential.

explanation.body: The potential at X is the sum of the contributions from $+Q$ at $3d$ and $-2Q$ at $d$, so $V_X=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0(3d)}+\frac{-2Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0d}=-\frac{5Q}{12\pi\varepsilon_0d}$. Multiplying by the charge placed at X gives $U=(3Q)V_X=-\frac{5Q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0d}$.

perOption.A: Uses the magnitude of the energy and loses the negative sign.
perOption.B: Correct. The negative source charge dominates the potential at X.
perOption.C: Uses an inverse-square dependence for potential energy.
perOption.D: Uses an inverse-square dependence and gives a positive energy.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A thundercloud and the Earth’s surface may be regarded as a pair of charged parallel plates separated by a distance $h$ as shown in the diagram. The capacitance of the system is $C$.

[Positive charges are marked along the flat base of the cloud, a vertical distance $h$ above the horizontal surface labelled Earth.]

What is the reduction in the electric field strength between the cloud and Earth when a lightning flash of mean current $I$ and time duration $t$ occurs?

A $\frac{It}{Ch}$
B $\frac{I}{Ch}$
C $CIt$
D $\frac{CIt}{h}$

stemImage.alt: Question 20: A thundercloud and the Earth’s surface may be regarded as a pair of charged parallel plates separated by a distance h as shown in the diagram. The capacitance o

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires chaining charge transfer, capacitance and uniform-field relations.
questions.misconception: Multiplying by capacitance to find the voltage change.

explanation.body: The charge transferred by the lightning flash is $\Delta Q=It$. Since $\Delta Q=C\Delta V$, the potential difference decreases by $It/C$. For parallel plates, $E=V/h$, so the field strength decreases by $\frac{It}{Ch}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses current in place of transferred charge by omitting the flash duration.
perOption.C: Multiplies the transferred charge by capacitance and omits division by plate separation.
perOption.D: Multiplies by capacitance where finding the potential difference requires division.
